meta.titre: Coastal Management Strategies: protecting a retreating shoreline
meta.sous_theme: Causes of coastal retreat and hard, soft and managed-retreat responses

sections.contenu_markdown: Along the Atlantic coast of Cameroon, towns such as Limbe, Douala and Kribi stand where the land meets the Gulf of Guinea. A beach, a belt of mangroves or a coastal road can be cut back by waves, and sand is often dug out of beaches for building. Whenever a shoreline moves inland, a community must decide whether to build a wall, add sand, plant vegetation or move away. The GCE asks both why a coast retreats and what people do about it, and it rewards answers that explain how each measure works and where it fails. This course gives you the causes, the strategies and the structure of an answer that earns the marks.

items: Waves are made by wind blowing over the sea, and larger waves carry more energy.
Longshore drift is the zig-zag movement of sand and pebbles along a beach in the direction of the prevailing waves.
Erosion wears away and removes material, while deposition drops the material that was being carried.
Weathering breaks down rock where it stands, without moving it.

sections.titre: Why coasts retreat and how people manage them
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Causes of coastal retreat
Coastal (shoreline) retreat is the landward movement of the line where land meets sea.

**Natural causes**
- **Wave erosion**: hydraulic action (the force of water and compressed air in cracks), abrasion (sand and pebbles hurled against the shore), attrition (carried material wears itself smaller) and solution (dissolving of soluble rock). Storm waves do most of the work.
- **Weathering and mass movement**: weakened cliffs slump or slide, especially when soaked by heavy rain.
- **Rising sea level and storm surges**: the same waves reach higher and further inland.
- **Weak geology**: loose sand, clay and gravel retreat much faster than hard rock.

**Human causes**: sand mining from beaches; dams that trap river sediment so less reaches the coast; clearing of mangroves and dune vegetation; harbour walls and jetties that block longshore drift; building too close to the shore.

### Management strategies
| Strategy | Type | How it works | Main limits |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sea wall | hard | a strong, often curved wall of concrete reflects wave energy | very costly; waves scour its base; the beach in front may disappear |
| Rock armour | hard | large boulders absorb and break up waves | cheaper than a wall but unsightly and boulders can shift |
| Groynes | hard | fences of wood or rock across the beach trap sand moved by longshore drift | starve the beach further along the coast, which then erodes faster |
| Gabions | hard | wire cages filled with stones absorb wave energy | short life because salt water corrodes the wire |
| Beach nourishment | soft | sand is added, so the wider beach absorbs waves | temporary; must be repeated and paid for again |
| Dune and mangrove planting | soft | roots bind sediment and the plants slow waves | slow to establish; need protection from people |
| Managed retreat | soft | the coast is allowed to flood and people are moved or compensated | loss of land, high social cost, resisted by owners |

Coastal planners choose between four broad options: **hold the line**, **advance the line**, **managed realignment** and **no active intervention**. A hard structure protects land strongly but can pass the problem along the coast. Soft methods work with natural processes, cost less over time and keep habitats, but give less certain protection.

variantes.nom: Two-part questions: causes and human efforts
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks for causes of retreat and for what people do to protect the coast.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Choose exactly the number asked. For each cause give the process and its effect (for example: storm waves use abrasion and hydraulic action at the base of the shore, so the beach narrows and the land behind is cut back). For each human effort name the measure, say how it works and add one limit. A bare list of names earns very little.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to examine, assess or discuss strategies, or to say which is best.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Describe how each strategy works, then judge it by cost, effectiveness, lifetime, effect on neighbouring coasts, effect on the environment and the value of the land protected. Compare hard and soft approaches and end with a reasoned judgement: for a valuable town a wall or rock armour may be justified, for a low-value rural shore planting or retreat is often more sensible.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question speaks of sustainable or long-term management of a whole coast.
variantes.contenu_markdown: This means managing the whole coastal zone, land and sea, with all users involved (fishers, residents, tourism, ports, authorities), mixing hard and soft methods, setting building limits behind the shore and banning sand mining where it causes retreat.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A fishing town stands on a low sandy coast. In 12 years the shoreline has retreated 30 m. A road lies 50 m inland of the present shoreline, with houses beyond it.

(a) Calculate the average yearly rate of retreat and the time before the shoreline reaches the road if the rate stays the same.
(b) Explain one hard and one soft strategy the council could use.
(c) Recommend and justify a choice. (10 marks)

etapes.action: Work out the average rate of retreat.
etapes.justification: A rate is distance divided by time, in metres per year.

etapes.action: Predict the time to reach the road.
etapes.justification: Time is distance divided by rate, assuming the rate is constant (storms can make real retreat faster).

etapes.action: Explain a hard strategy: rock armour along the shore.
etapes.justification: Name the method, say how it works, and give its limit; this is the pattern for every strategy.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Large boulders are piled along the base of the beach. Waves break on the rocks and lose energy instead of cutting the shore. It protects the road well and is easier to repair than a concrete wall. However it is costly, hides the beach, and may push erosion onto the unprotected neighbouring coast.

etapes.action: Explain a soft strategy: beach nourishment with planting.
etapes.justification: Soft methods work with natural processes and must be shown as active management, not as doing nothing.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Sand is pumped or trucked onto the beach, giving a wider beach that absorbs wave energy, and mangroves or grasses are planted behind it so roots bind the sand. It keeps the beach for fishing boats and recreation and is cheaper to start, but it is temporary and must be repeated after storms.

etapes.justification: Evaluation questions need a judgement based on criteria, not only descriptions.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Since the road and houses are valuable and the shoreline could reach the road in about 20 years, rock armour at the most threatened section is justified, combined with nourishment and planting elsewhere to reduce cost and damage to neighbouring beaches.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The shoreline retreats at **2.5 m per year** and could reach the road in about **20 years**. A model answer combines rock armour (strong, costly, may transfer erosion) with nourishment and planting (cheaper, natural, temporary) and recommends a mixed plan backed by reasons.

items.erreur_markdown: "The council can build sea walls, groynes and gabions." (a list of names and nothing else)
items.pourquoi_faux: A list of names shows recall but not understanding. Each strategy needs to be explained to earn marks.
items.correction_markdown: For each strategy say what it is, how it reduces wave energy or traps sediment, and one limit, for example that groynes starve the beach further along the coast.

items.erreur_markdown: "Groynes stop erosion along the whole coast."
items.pourquoi_faux: Groynes trap sand on the side from which longshore drift arrives. The beach beyond them receives less sand, so it can erode faster.
items.correction_markdown: Say that groynes build a beach where they are placed but may increase erosion down the drift direction.

items.pourquoi_faux: Soft engineering is active management that works with natural processes (nourishment, dune and mangrove planting). Doing nothing is a different option.
items.correction_markdown: Define soft engineering as low-impact methods that use or imitate natural defences, and treat no active intervention as a separate choice.

items.erreur_markdown: "Once a sea wall is built the coast is protected for ever."
items.pourquoi_faux: Hard structures wear out, need maintenance, and can fail in storms. Waves also scour the base of a wall.
items.correction_markdown: State the useful lifetime and the maintenance cost, and mention effects on neighbouring beaches.

items.pourquoi_faux: This is too vague for an explanation mark. It does not name a process.
items.correction_markdown: Name the process, for example abrasion by sand and pebbles thrown at the shore, or hydraulic action in cracks, and state its effect on the shoreline.

items.enonce_markdown: Classify each of these as hard engineering, soft engineering or managed retreat: (a) rock armour; (b) mangrove planting; (c) groynes; (d) moving houses away from an eroding shore; (e) beach nourishment; (f) a concrete sea wall. Then name one disadvantage of hard engineering.
items.solution_markdown: (a) **hard**; (b) **soft**; (c) **hard**; (d) **managed retreat**; (e) **soft**; (f) **hard**. One disadvantage of hard engineering: it is costly and can increase erosion on neighbouring unprotected coast (a wall can also be undermined at its base).

items.enonce_markdown: A council compares two options for 400 m of shoreline over 30 years. Option A, a sea wall: construction costs 1,800,000 FCFA per metre, and yearly maintenance is 1% of the construction cost. Option B, beach nourishment: 150,000,000 FCFA each time, repeated every 5 years, starting now. (a) Calculate the total cost of each option over 30 years. (b) State which is cheaper in money and give two other factors the council should consider. (All costs are illustrative.)
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Option A: construction $400 \times 1\,800\,000 = 720\,000\,000$ FCFA. Maintenance per year is $1\% \times 720\,000\,000 = 7\,200\,000$ FCFA, so over 30 years $7\,200\,000 \times 30 = 216\,000\,000$ FCFA. Total **936,000,000 FCFA**.
Option B: $30 \div 5 = 6$ rounds, so $6 \times 150\,000\,000 = $ **900,000,000 FCFA**.

(b) Option B is cheaper in money by 36,000,000 FCFA, a small difference. The council should also consider the effect on neighbouring beaches (a wall can pass erosion along the coast), the value of the beach for fishing and tourism, the risk of storm damage, and the lifespan of each option.

items.enonce_markdown: On a straight sandy coast, longshore drift moves sand from west to east. A harbour jetty is built across the beach at the western edge of a town. After ten years the beach west of the jetty is very wide, but the town beach to the east has lost much of its sand and the shore is retreating. (a) Explain what has happened. (b) Suggest and evaluate two ways of managing the problem.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Award marks for: the jetty blocks the sand carried by longshore drift; sand accumulates on the west (up-drift) side, widening the beach; sand no longer reaches the east (down-drift) side, while waves continue to carry sand away, so the beach narrows; a thin beach gives less protection, so waves reach the shore and erode it, and the land retreats.

(b) Any two, each explained and evaluated: **sand bypassing** (sand from the west side is pumped or trucked across to the east beach; restores the natural supply but needs repeated cost); **beach nourishment** on the eastern beach (cheap to start, temporary); **groynes or rock armour** on the eastern shore (protect strongly, but may shift erosion further east); **dune or mangrove planting** (natural, low cost, slow). A strong answer ends by recommending a combination, such as bypassing with planting, and justifies it.

items_markdown: Coasts retreat because of wave erosion (hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition, solution), weathering and mass movement, rising sea level and storms, and human actions such as sand mining, dams, mangrove clearance and structures that block longshore drift.
Hard engineering (sea walls, rock armour, groynes, gabions) gives strong protection but is costly, wears out and can shift erosion to neighbouring coasts.
Soft engineering (beach nourishment, dune and mangrove planting) and managed retreat work with natural processes; they cost less over time and keep habitats but protect less certainly.
The four planning options are hold the line, advance the line, managed realignment and no active intervention.
In answers explain each strategy (what it is, how it works, one limit) and, when asked to examine, end with a reasoned judgement.
